statement: A symmetric matrix is a square matrix that is equal to its transpose: $A = A^{\mathsf{T}}$, or equivalently in terms of its entries, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all row indices $i$ and column indices $j$.

symbols.meaning: entry in the i-th row and j-th column of matrix A
number of rows and columns of the matrix

properties.property: Entries across the main diagonal are equal: $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $1 \leq i, j \leq n$.
properties.why: Transposition swaps row and column indices while matrix equality requires corresponding entries to match.

properties.property: An $n \times n$ symmetric matrix is determined by $\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)$ scalars.
properties.why: Only the entries on or above the main diagonal can be chosen independently.

properties.property: The sum and difference of two symmetric matrices are symmetric.
properties.why: Transposition distributes linearly over matrix addition and subtraction.

properties.property: The product $AB$ of symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$ is symmetric if and only if $A$ and $B$ commute ($AB = BA$).
properties.why: Taking the transpose yields $(AB)^{\mathsf{T}} = B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}} = BA$, which equals $AB$ precisely when $AB = BA$.

properties.property: If $A$ is symmetric, then $A^k$ is symmetric for any integer $k \geq 0$, and $A^{-1}$ (if it exists) is symmetric.
properties.why: Transposition commutes with integer powers and matrix inversion.

properties.property: Any matrix congruent to a symmetric matrix is symmetric ($PAP^{\mathsf{T}}$ is symmetric for any matrix $P$).
A real $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is symmetric if and only if $\langle Ax, y \rangle = \langle x, Ay \rangle$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with respect to the standard inner product.
properties.why: A real symmetric matrix represents a self-adjoint operator over a real inner product space.

properties.property: Every real symmetric matrix can be diagonalized by an orthogonal matrix $Q$ such that $D = Q^{\mathsf{T}}AQ$ is diagonal, and all of its eigenvalues are real.
properties.why: Every real symmetric matrix is Hermitian and normal, satisfying the finite-dimensional spectral theorem.

properties.property: The rank of a symmetric matrix $A$ is equal to the number of non-zero eigenvalues of $A$.
properties.why: Symmetric matrices are diagonalizable up to choice of basis.

assumptions.breaks_when: The matrix has unequal dimensions ($m \times n$ with $m \neq n$), because equal matrices must have identical dimensions.

assumptions.assumption: The underlying scalar field has characteristic different from 2 (for Toeplitz decomposition into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts).
assumptions.breaks_when: The field has characteristic 2, where $1 = -1$ and division by 2 is undefined.

failure_modes.mode: Loss of symmetry under matrix multiplication
failure_modes.signature: Product matrix satisfies $AB \neq (AB)^{\mathsf{T}}$ despite $A = A^{\mathsf{T}}$ and $B = B^{\mathsf{T}}$.
failure_modes.cause: The symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$ do not commute ($AB \neq BA$).

failure_modes.mode: Defectiveness under similarity for complex symmetric matrices
failure_modes.signature: Jordan normal form contains non-trivial Jordan blocks, preventing diagonalization via similarity transformation.
failure_modes.cause: A general complex symmetric matrix is not necessarily Hermitian and may lack a complete basis of eigenvectors.
